items.stem: An agent reads the company wiki, summarises uploaded customer files and can post to any webhook URL. What is the main risk?

options.text: Slow responses, because three tools add latency.
options.feedback: Latency is a real cost, but it is not the main risk here. The tool combination creates a security problem.

options.text: An instruction hidden in an uploaded file can make it post wiki content to an attacker's URL.
options.feedback: Correct. Private data, untrusted content and external communication meet on one identity, which is the lethal trifecta.

options.text: The wiki tool alone is dangerous because it reads private data.
options.feedback: Reading private data is one leg. On its own it cannot send anything out or be steered by outside text.

options.text: No risk, as long as the system prompt forbids sharing wiki content.
options.feedback: A prompt is not a control. Injected text in the upload competes with that instruction and can win.

items.explanation: All three legs sit on one identity. Breaking any one, such as removing the webhook tool or quarantining uploads, removes the exfiltration path.

items.stem: An inbox agent must read inbound email and the CRM. Which changes break the lethal trifecta while keeping those tools? Select all that apply.

options.text: Remove the send tool so the agent saves drafts for the account owner.
options.feedback: Correct. Without a way to send, the external-communication leg is gone.

options.text: Have a no-tools model extract sender, intent and order number from each email into a schema.
options.feedback: Correct. The planner never reads attacker-written text, which neutralises the untrusted-content leg.

options.text: Require the account owner to approve the exact recipient and body of every outbound message.
options.feedback: Correct. Nothing leaves without a person seeing the real effect, which breaks the external leg.

options.text: Tell the model in its system prompt never to email CRM data.
options.feedback: Incorrect. This is an instruction, not a structural change, and injected text can override it.

options.text: Switch to a larger model that follows instructions better.
options.feedback: Incorrect. A stronger model may resist some attacks, but every leg is still present.

items.explanation: Each correct option removes one leg by structure. Prompt wording and model choice leave all three legs in place.

items.stem: A user asks an agent to summarise a supplier's web page. The page contains hidden text telling the agent to email its contact list to an outside address. What is this?

options.text: Direct prompt injection.
options.feedback: Not quite. Direct injection comes from the person typing, and this user made an ordinary request.

options.text: Indirect prompt injection.
options.feedback: Correct. The instruction arrived inside content the agent read, not from its user.

options.text: A hallucination.
options.feedback: Incorrect. The model did not invent anything; an attacker planted the instruction in the page.

options.text: Not an attack, because the user is authenticated.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Authentication says who asked, not who wrote the content the agent reads.

items.explanation: Indirect injection rides in through pages, emails, files and tool descriptions. The trusted user unknowingly delivers it.

items.stem: Which are structural defences against prompt injection? Select all that apply.

options.text: A quarantined model with no tools that returns only schema-validated fields.
options.feedback: Correct. Attacker text cannot call tools, and only typed values leave the quarantine.

options.text: Authorising every tool call in the gateway and the database under the principal's identity.
options.feedback: Correct. Even a persuaded model cannot perform an action the principal is not allowed.

options.text: Accepting only order IDs that match a known pattern and exist for this customer.
options.feedback: Correct. Typed, allowlisted values give injected sentences nowhere to go.

options.text: A system prompt line saying to ignore instructions inside documents.
options.feedback: Incorrect as a sufficient defence. It is still an instruction, and it offers no guarantee.

options.text: Writing the system prompt in capital letters so it takes priority.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Emphasis changes nothing structural, and attacker text can use the same trick.

items.explanation: Structural defences limit what a successful injection can do. Instruction-only defences try to persuade the model, which an attacker can also do.

items.stem: A team requires approval for all 6,000 daily agent actions. Approval rate is 99.8 per cent and median decision time is two seconds. What is the best next step?

options.text: Hire more reviewers so each one approves fewer actions.
options.feedback: This spreads the load but keeps people reviewing actions that do not need them, so fatigue persists.

options.text: Move reversible low-value actions to logged or sampled review, and keep approval for irreversible, external or high-value ones.
options.feedback: Correct. Fewer, meaningful approvals give reviewers time to read the actions that matter.

options.text: Remove all gates, since reviewers approve nearly everything anyway.
options.feedback: Too far. The rare costly actions still need a person, even if most actions do not.

options.text: Keep the design, because a high approval rate shows the agent is reliable.
options.feedback: Two-second decisions suggest rubber-stamping, not careful review. The gates are no longer working.

items.explanation: Approval fatigue makes every gate weaker. Placing gates by reversibility, external effect and value keeps them meaningful.

items.stem: Order these agent actions from the lightest gate to the strictest.

items.text: Delete a customer's account at their request.
Change payout bank details because an email asked.
Refund $15 on a delivered-damaged order within policy.

items.explanation: Reading public data runs automatically. A small refund runs with sampled review. Deletion is irreversible, so it needs approval first. Bank detail changes from email are never left to an agent.

items.stem: An agent must answer customers' questions about their own order status. Which design follows least agency?

options.text: A planner agent with a general SQL tool on the orders database.
options.feedback: Too much agency and too broad a tool. A general query tool can reach every customer's data.

options.text: A single read-only get_order_status call scoped to the signed-in customer, with a short-lived token.
options.feedback: Correct. It is the lowest sufficient level, with one narrow, read-only tool and a scoped credential.

options.text: A bounded loop with order lookup, refund and email tools, in case customers ask for more.
options.feedback: Tools added in case are not earned by the requirement. Refund and email widen what an injection could do.

options.text: Any design, as long as the agent's service account has broad but audited access.
options.feedback: Auditing records misuse after the fact. Broad access still lets one injection reach everything.

items.explanation: Least agency picks the lowest level and the narrowest tools that meet the requirement, with read-only defaults and scoped, short-lived credentials.

items.stem: Which statement about the NIST AI RMF 1.0 is accurate?

options.text: It is voluntary guidance organised into four functions: Govern, Map, Measure and Manage.
options.feedback: Correct. Organisations adopt it to structure how they identify, assess and treat AI risk.

options.text: It is a certifiable management-system standard.
options.feedback: That describes ISO/IEC 42001, which specifies requirements for an AI management system.

options.text: It is a regulation that bans prohibited AI practices.
options.feedback: That describes part of the EU AI Act, which is a risk-based regulation.

options.text: It applies only to general-purpose AI models.
options.feedback: Incorrect. It is a general framework for managing risk across AI systems.

items.explanation: The three frameworks are different instruments: voluntary guidance, a certifiable standard and a regulation. Each asks for evidence engineering can supply.

items.stem: An auditor asks how your agent provides human oversight. Which artefact is the strongest evidence?

options.text: A policy statement saying humans oversee the system.
options.feedback: A statement of intent is weak evidence. It does not show how or where oversight happens.

options.text: The gate design, listing which actions need approval, plus logs of approvals and rejections.
options.feedback: Correct. It shows the designed control and records that it runs in production.

options.text: The latest eval report on answer accuracy.
options.feedback: Eval reports are good evidence for accuracy, but they say little about human oversight.

options.text: The model provider's terms of service.
options.feedback: These describe the provider's obligations, not how your system involves people in decisions.

items.explanation: Map each expectation to an artefact: oversight to gate design and approval logs, accuracy to eval reports, logging to traces, risk to the register.

items.stem: An agent starts emailing CRM data to unknown domains. Put the response stages in order.

items.text: Read the traces to find the input and tool calls that caused the leak.
Add the hostile input to the golden set as a regression case.
An alert fires on outbound mail to previously unseen domains.
Disable the send tool and revoke the agent's CRM token.
Quarantine inbound email and gate outbound attachments.
Hold a blameless post-incident review and update the risk register.

items.explanation: Containment comes before investigation so nothing else leaks. The regression case stops the failure returning, and the blameless review feeds governance.
